title: Prescriptive analytics for human resource planning in the professional services industry
contribution: A two-stage affinely adaptive robust LP for consulting-firm hiring and staffing under uncertain deal forecasts (hires now; contractors, transfers and fulfilment adapt), compared on one quarter of Sapient data, through 500 simulated realizations, with a deterministic LP equivalent to a practice-like greedy rule and with a static robust LP.
problem_entry: {RO AP} Hiring must precede contract closure by about a quarter on uncertain forecasts; prediction-only and point-estimate staffing work exists; stochastic programming is judged impractical (curse of dimensionality, distributions hard to estimate); no affinely adaptive RO model had been applied to HR planning (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: A deterministic LP over requests x channels is shown equivalent to a greedy rule that the authors expect mimics ad hoc practice (pp. 2-3); a robust version uses an l1-norm set around the forecasts (p. 3); a two-stage version makes contractors y(u), transfers z(u) and fulfilment w(u) affine in realized requests, with the static robust model as a special case (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Continuous staffing (part-time allowed); contractors dearer than new hires; bench cost zero (pp. 2-3); a one-standard-deviation l1 set, two standard deviations judged over-conservative (p. 4); one quarter of Sapient financial-services data, travel-plus-training transfer costs, three business units solved separately (p. 4).
proof_devices: feasible-direction argument that the greedy Algorithm 1 is optimal for the deterministic LP (p. 3)
affine decision rules as the tractable restriction of fully adaptive policies (p. 3)
robust counterpart delegated to JuMPeR; the class of the counterpart is not stated (p. 4)
experiments: 500 simulations per method with normal noise sigma = 0.5d and the second stage re-solved; Julia/JuMP/JuMPeR on a laptop (p. 4); adaptive run times 1,327.1-1,832.6 s against <= 3.4 s for the others (Table 2, p. 5); the adaptive plan dominates in North America (mean $14.05M vs $12.66M deterministic and $12.76M robust), while the deterministic plan keeps the highest mean in Europe and India and the adaptive plan raises min and CVaR and lowers sd (Table 3, p. 5); India's small gains are explained by low labor and transfer costs (pp. 5-6).
positioning: Set against stochastic programming and prediction-only sales analytics; extends affinely adaptive RO (Ben-Tal et al. 2004; Bertsimas-Goyal; Bertsimas-Iancu-Parrilo) to HR planning, where it is claimed not to have been applied (p. 2).
writing: Two-item contribution list (p. 2); an informal greedy reading of the LP as a stand-in for practice (p. 3); results narrated per business unit with a structural explanation of the null case (pp. 5-6); the conclusion credits the adaptive plan with good expected performance and generality beyond what Table 3 shows (pp. 5-6).
limits_future: Simplified two-stage timeline; multi-period and hiring-calendar extensions described, not built (p. 4); realizations simulated from the model's own noise family (p. 4); the adaptive mean beats the deterministic mean only in North America (Table 3, p. 5); no deployment reported.

method_links.note: Partner data, a partner committee and a decision metric (profit distribution, CVaR) are present, but the baseline is a deterministic plan the authors expect mimics practice, not an observed current rule; no field test.

The set width (in standard deviations) is chosen against over-conservatism, and the bad case is printed: the robust plan loses mean and median profit in Europe and India; the India null result is explained (Heuristic 4).

transferable: Show that the nominal LP is solved by a simple greedy rule that mirrors practice, and use that rule as the interpretable baseline the robust and adaptive plans must beat (p. 3).
Score a here-and-now plan by re-solving the recourse on many realizations; report min, CVaR at 0.1, median, mean and sd per segment next to run times (pp. 4-5).
When a segment shows no gain, explain it by the cost structure that makes recourse cheap there (pp. 5-6).
coauthors: Lauren Berk, Alexander M. Weinstein, Julia Yan

quotes.text: This conservatism is well-suited to robust optimization, which considers worst-case cost rather than expected cost.

However, the robust method could be seen as over-conservative: although the median and mean robust profits are slightly better than the deterministic profits in North America, these metrics are significantly worse in Europe and India.

title: Certifiably optimal sparse principal component analysis
contribution: Optimal-SPCA, a custom branch-and-bound over support indicators with linear-algebra bounds (masked eigenvalue, truncated trace, Gershgorin sums) and a Yuan-Zhang primal heuristic, certifies l0-constrained sparse PCA optima where a general MINLP solver fails, finds the optimum as fast as heuristics, and proves optimality for most k = 5 problems up to 10,000 dimensions.
problem_entry: {ML IO} Dense PCA loadings hurt interpretability and variable selection; relaxations, first-order methods and earlier exact attempts give no certificate or are too slow; the why-now is the MIO speed-up (solvers about 1,250,000 times faster, 2 trillion with hardware, 1990-2016); the l0-constrained form is chosen over penalized and l1 forms (pp. 2-7).
key_idea: Branch on the support indicators of SPCA-MIO with nodes (l, u); bound nodes by lambda_max of the masked matrix, the truncated trace and Gershgorin sums (upper) and by eigenvector truncation and an adapted Yuan-Zhang truncated power iteration (lower); stop at epsilon-optimality (pp. 8-17).
assumptions: Any PSD covariance of centered data, correlation versions too (p. 26); data Pitprops, Wine, MiniBooNE, Communities, breast-cancer gene expression (random subsets up to 10,000 variables) and Micromass (pp. 25-26, 33); parameters tuned on 500 draws of 80 of Communities' 101 variables (p. 18).
proof_devices: correctness and finite termination of the branch-and-bound: nodes in {0,1}^{2n}, only dominated or partitioned nodes removed (Theorem 1, p. 12)
upper bounds from support relaxation (masked matrix), the trace inequality and the Gershgorin theorem, maximized over feasible supports through a truncation routine (pp. 13-16)
non-redundancy of two bounds shown by two 3x3 matrices (p. 18)
deflation for later components, without joint optimality (p. 12)
experiments: Certified optimum on every data set at k = 5 and 10 while every competitor misses at least one (Tables 6-7, pp. 26-28); proofs up to 167 s at Communities k = 10 (Table 10, p. 32); Couenne 0.5 on the same formulation often runs over an hour with huge gaps, against at most 339 s (Table 11, p. 34); k = 5 scaling to 10,000 dimensions with 91-100% proved within 1 h (Table 12, p. 34); early termination ties Yuan-Zhang in 94.5-99% of runs (Table 13, p. 36); Julia without a solver, run times confounded by language (pp. 25, 31); Table 6 lists a competitor above the asterisked optimum on Communities k = 5 without comment (p. 27).
positioning: Joins the literature reconsidering statistics and ML problems through modern optimization (p. 3); reviews four SPCA formulations, first-order methods (fast, no certificate, good warm starts), preprocessing, parallelism and earlier exact attempts (Moghaddam et al. too slow; Carrizosa-Guerrero only local) (pp. 4-6).
writing: Three numbered claims (p. 7) restated in the computational conclusions (p. 35); argues the l0-constrained form against l1 shrinkage (pp. 6-7); the abstract promises proofs in seconds for n in the hundreds and k in the tens, while the body reports minutes at k = 10 (pp. 1, 31-34).
limits_future: Proof time grows with k (p. 31); no joint optimality over several components (pp. 12, 29); scaling tested only at k = 5 (p. 33); run-time comparisons confounded by language (p. 31); Communities used for both tuning and testing (pp. 18, 26); future: node bookkeeping, eigenvalue reuse as warm starts for lower nodes (p. 36), parallel branch-and-bound (p. 5).

method_links.note: The fastest incumbent heuristic (Yuan-Zhang) is both the node lower-bound routine and the strongest opponent; certificates from Theorem 1; time-to-best reported apart from time-to-proof with the share proved in 1 h and 5 h; wins and ties stated; code released.

The solver x hardware figure (1,250,000; 2 trillion, 1990-2016) is the why-now, but Optimal-SPCA uses no MIO solver and the general solver tested fails: the figure is borrowed, not measured on the tool used (Method 2 checkpoint).
The exact SPCA-MIO is nonconvex and leaves solver classes; a special-purpose exact algorithm built from linear-algebra bounds replaces a class-keeping device.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact special-purpose algorithm when the formulation leaves solver classes
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Custom branch-and-bound with closed-form linear-algebra bounds after Couenne fails on SPCA-MIO; S303 does the same with closed-form worst cases and enumeration.

transferable: For a cardinality-constrained eigenvalue problem, branch on support indicators and bound each node by cheap linear-algebra quantities (masked lambda_max, truncated trace, Gershgorin sums through one truncation routine), taking the minimum (pp. 13-18).
Show that two bounds are non-redundant with two tiny matrices, each dominated by the other bound (p. 18).
Run the fastest heuristic as the node lower-bound routine, so the exact method never does worse than the heuristic and adds a certificate (pp. 17, 25).
Report time-to-best and time-to-proof separately with the share of runs proved in 1 h and in 5 h, and run a general solver on the same formulation to justify a custom algorithm (Tables 11-12, p. 34).

quotes.text: These speedups encourage us to rethink whether NP-hardness should in fact be synonymous with intractability.
None of these methods provide a certificate of optimality, but are very useful as warm starts for exact methods.

title: Robust maximum likelihood estimation
contribution: Robust maximum likelihood estimators against adversarial (uncertainty-set) and distributional (bounded-support) data errors, computed by a Danskin-gradient robust local search with per-sample trust-region inner problems and by robust simulated annealing, which in simulation degrade less than nominal MLE inside an error-size window and on 491 radiation-therapy plans give more sample-stable estimates.
problem_entry: {RO ML; HS as global search; AP} MLE assumes error-free data, and errors of several kinds can erase its advantages; the entry is to maximize the worst-case likelihood, unlike Huber's estimator-side robustness (pp. 2-3, Table 1).
key_idea: The ARE maximizes over theta the minimum over per-sample l2-ball errors of the log-likelihood (p. 4); a Danskin gradient at the inner worst case drives the 2010 robust local search (p. 5); Gaussian data make the inner problem separate into trust-region problems (pp. 5-6); robust SA gives a global estimator (p. 6); the DRE reduces to an ARE with one shared error and is less conservative (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: Errors much smaller than data, for identifiability; semiparametric (p. 4); simulated n = 400 samples in R^4 with 40 error matrices, normal then uniform-ball errors (pp. 7, 11); 491 delivered IMRT plans, 18 tumor sites, five DVH points, same protocol and software; normality justified by patient independence (pp. 12-13).
proof_devices: descent-direction theorem for the worst-case cost restated from Bertsimas-Nohadani-Teo 2010 (Theorem 1, p. 5)
Danskin's theorem for the gradient of the inner minimum (eq. (10), p. 5)
per-sample separability into trust-region problems solved by Ye's O(log log(1/eps)) method (pp. 5-6)
projection of the descent direction to keep Sigma PSD (p. 6)
reduction of the distributionally robust problem with a common bounded support to an adversarial one with a shared error (eq. (16), p. 6)
experiments: Robust beats nominal log-likelihood by up to 10% (ARE) and 15% (DRE) for rho >= 1 (p. 8); an effectiveness window in a delta x rho grid (pp. 9-10); robust SA beats a 100-start local search for delta > 0.3 at about 215 s against 100 s (p. 10); uniform errors give similar trends (p. 11); factor analysis is better on covariances (p. 11); clinical subsampling (3,000 samples of 50 plans; an 80-sample check): robust means stable up to rho <= 2 Gy, Sigma_rob(D95, D2) narrower but worse for rho <= 0.8 (pp. 13-14).
positioning: Contrasted with Huber's robust statistics in a table (p. 3); builds on El Ghaoui-Lebret and Calafiore-El Ghaoui (robust least squares and MLE in linear models) and on the authors' robust local search and robust SA (pp. 3, 5-6).
writing: Broad application framing (finance, medical decisions, clinical trials) (p. 2); the negative factor-analysis result stated plainly in the summary (p. 12); the conclusion claims direct applicability to a wide variety of settings (p. 14).
limits_future: Identifiability out of scope (p. 4); benefit only inside an error-size window (p. 12); worse than a correct parametric model (p. 12); other organs deferred to a dosimetric study (p. 12); savings in clinical-trial sample size (p. 14) and robustness to overfitting (p. 7) asserted, not tested; in simulation rho* is chosen against the true data (p. 10).

method_links.note: One knob (Gamma, scanned as rho) with its effectiveness window printed at both failing ends and a clinical region where robust is worse; variant: in simulation the knob is set against the true data, not from data alone.
The robust MLE leaves convex classes; tractability comes from separable trust-region inner problems, first-order outer steps and SA, with no LP, conic or MIO counterpart.
Delivered clinical plans with the institution's nominal estimators as baseline, but the score is estimator spread, not decisions or outcomes; clinical value is argued.

transferable: Differentiate a max-min objective by Danskin's theorem, evaluating the gradient at the inner worst case only (eq. (10), p. 5).
Exploit separability over samples: with a Gaussian likelihood and l2-ball errors each sample's worst case is a trust-region problem (pp. 5-6).
Map a robust method's range of effectiveness on an error-size x set-size grid against ground truth, printing both the too-small and the too-large end (pp. 9-10, 12).
Pit the method against a correctly specified parametric competitor and print where the competitor wins (p. 11).

quotes.text: In data-driven applications, the analysis of the dip can be used reversely to motivate the appropriate size of the uncertainty set

This demonstrates that although robust maximum likelihood estimation offers advantages to estimates of uncertain input data, it underperforms when the data-generating process is known and can be leveraged.

title: Robust and stochastic formulations for ambulance deployment and dispatch
contribution: Two-stage stochastic and robust ambulance deployment models with fully adaptive integer dispatch recourse and a hierarchical Poisson-quantile uncertainty set, solved exactly through recourse duality, binary expansion and column-and-constraint generation; on Washington DC data they cut shortfalls by about 22% at 50 ambulances against MEXCLP and MALP and match those models' 50-ambulance performance with 35.
problem_entry: {RO IO AP} Covering models ignore busy ambulances or assume constant busy fractions; robust static models restrict dispatch and are conservative; fully adaptive models are intractable; C&CG and better EMS data reopen exact adaptive models without repositioning (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: The recourse is the minimum shortfall under in-period optimal dispatch (p. 3); stochastic and robust first-stage models (pp. 3-4); D(alpha) bounds single-region, neighbourhood, catchment and city demand by Poisson quantiles (p. 4); recourse duality, binary expansion and big-M give an MILP oracle inside C&CG (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: Integer deployment and dispatch; Poisson counts, called not fundamental; no probabilistic guarantee; alpha by cross-validation (pp. 4, 7); 179,160 DC EMS records, 3 months to build and 12 to test, weekdays, 217 regions, 10-minute OpenStreetMap drivetime (p. 6); closest available dispatch, no chute time, lognormal turnaround in three regimes (pp. 6-7).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: any scenario lies in D(alpha) for alpha small enough (p. 4; proof p. 9)
Proposition 2: recourse duality turning the robust recourse into a bilinear maximization (p. 4; proof p. 9)
binary expansion of integer scenarios and big-M linearization into an MILP (p. 5)
finite convergence of C&CG via Zeng-Zhao (Propositions 3-4, pp. 6, 9)
experiments: Gurobi 6.0 and JuMP on a laptop; the stochastic deterministic equivalent with 500 scenarios takes about a minute; C&CG converges in fewer than 20 iterations and all robust runs finish within 10 minutes (p. 8); MEXCLP and MALP with q cross-validated to 0.654 (p. 8); fleets of 10-50, peak and off-peak, three turnaround regimes (pp. 6-7); at 50 ambulances shortfalls of 3.7 and 3.53 against 4.36 and 4.89 (about 22%), response times about 34.6% better at peak and 23% off-peak; gains only when the busy fraction is below 1; stochastic close to robust (p. 8); 35 ambulances match the probabilistic models' 50, about $7 million a year (pp. 8-9); per-fleet tables are images (pp. 11-14).
positioning: Against the covering-model lineage (SCLP, MCLP, MEXCLP, MALP), chance-constrained or restricted-dispatch robust models and real-time redeployment work; credits Zeng-Zhao C&CG and Gabrel et al.'s linearization (pp. 1-2).
writing: Four-item contribution list (p. 2); results translated into operational and money terms (pp. 8-9); the abstract leads with exact optimality within minutes and a 19 to 28% shortfall reduction (p. 1).
limits_future: The best alpha is city-specific, so no general prescription (p. 7); saturation for alpha above 0.01 (p. 11); closest-idle dispatch assumed (pp. 2, 6); no field implementation, and the baselines are literature models rather than the agency's plan; future: real-time redeployment on top (p. 9).

method_links.note: A two-stage robust problem with integer recourse is kept in MILP by duality, binary expansion and big-M and solved exactly by C&CG with measured times; the intermediate MIQP is called hard in general.
One knob alpha scales all quantile bounds and is set by cross-validation on held-out data (the data-set knob of Method 3's correction); saturation is printed.

Decisions are scored by simulated shortfall and response time on 12 held-out months and translated into money, but the baselines are tuned literature models, not the agency's deployment; no field test.
The why-now is an algorithmic advance (C&CG) plus better data, not a measured solver x hardware figure.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 35 ambulances reach the probabilistic models' 50-ambulance performance, about $7 million a year; also S231 (children spared CT at an equal miss rate) and S303 (subjects needed for 80% power).

transferable: Build a data-driven polyhedral uncertainty set by bounding demand at several aggregation levels with Poisson quantiles and one alpha scaling all of them; bounds at a single level either concentrate adversarial demand or overstate the total (p. 4).
For integer recourse: dualize the recourse, write integer scenarios as sums of binary vectors, linearize the bilinear terms with big-M and run C&CG (pp. 4-5).
Tune the baseline fairly by cross-validating the competing models' parameter on the same data; train on the first months and test on the following year (pp. 6, 8).
Use a load statistic (here the busy fraction) to state when the method helps (p. 8).

quotes.text: The approach is data-driven, and does not rely on model-driven assumptions to provide any probabilistic guarantees on the resulting coverage provided by the model.
This is expected as the stochastic and robust formulations consider the dispatch decisions, whereas the MEXCLP and MALP do not.

title: Comparison of machine learning optimal classification trees with the pediatric emergency care applied research network head trauma decision rules
contribution: OCT-based risk rules refit on PECARN's public head-trauma cohort and tuned to PECARN's miss rate raise validation specificity (69.3% vs 52.8% under 2 years; 65.6% vs 57.6% from 2 years) with no significant loss of sensitivity, so more children could be spared CT.
problem_entry: {ML AP} CT is costly and irradiating; the PECARN rules are widely used and validated but simple; the entry is that simplicity may cost accuracy and that memorability is unnecessary where EHR decision support exists (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Refit with optimal classification trees on PECARN's data, weighting true positives 500 times false positives to match PECARN's miss rate, with PECARN-aligned risk cutoffs (1/1000, 3/100) and optimization-based imputation (p. 3).
assumptions: 42,412 children, 25 EDs, 2004-2006, GCS 14-15, two age strata; random development/validation split; 980 non-operational altered-mental-status labels treated as not altered; missing completely at random checked by logistic regressions (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: n/a: no formulation of its own; paired odds ratios and ratios of likelihood ratios with 95% CIs (p. 3)
experiments: Validation specificity 69.3% vs 52.8% and 65.6% vs 57.6%; sensitivity, NPV and LR- not significantly different (p. 1; Table 3, p. 6); misses 0 vs 1 and 10 vs 9 (pp. 1, 4); 32% fewer younger children in the CT group (p. 4); CART and complete-case analyses called congruent but not shown (p. 4); count labels swapped on p. 4, and the older-stratum gain given as 14% (p. 4) and 8% (p. 6).
positioning: Secondary analysis of PECARN's data; presents OCT as an alternative to the CART-derived rules and leaves the choice to clinicians' preference for simple rules or personalized risks (pp. 2, 7-8).
writing: JAMA structured abstract and Key Points (pp. 1-2); hedged clinical claims next to a methods claim that MIO fitting provably outperforms CART fitting (pp. 1, 3, 8); an explicit Limitations section (p. 8).
limits_future: No external validation; internal validation no substitute; a prospective implementation is needed; the trees cannot be memorized and need the EHR; the effect on CT use is unknown since PECARN's own effect is unproven (p. 8); a web tool is provided (p. 8).

method_links.note: The opponent is the field's deployed rule, met on its own development data at a matched miss rate; the paper states that accuracy is a surrogate and that external and prospective validation are needed.
The CART duel exists only as an unreported sensitivity analysis; no solver, time limit or certificate status is given for the trees, while MIO fitting is said to provably outperform CART fitting.
The clinical result goes to a clinical journal with a web tool (Workflow E); Bertsimas obtained the funding and co-supervised.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: More very-low-risk children identified (fewer CT scans) at the incumbent's miss rate; also S224 (ambulances) and S303 (trial subjects).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: clinical pipeline: optimal imputation, OCT, public web tool
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimization-based imputation before OCT and a web tool to show use; S281 uses OptImpute, OptimalTrees and a webpage and app.

transferable: Tune the new classifier to the incumbent's miss rate (here by weighting positives 500 times) and compete on the other error, with paired ratios and CIs (pp. 3, 6).
Use the incumbent's own public data and its own risk cutoffs so that only the model differs (pp. 2-3).
Say in the paper that predictive accuracy is a surrogate and list the studies still needed: external validation, prospective implementation, outcomes (pp. 4, 8).
coauthors: Jack Dunn, Dale W. Steele, Thomas A. Trikalinos, Yuchen Wang

quotes.text: improvements in predictive accuracy will not benefit patients unless the new tools are used in practice and lead to changes in diagnostic thinking and patient management
For these reasons, it is debatable whether the PECARN rules’ apparent simplicity is always worth its price.

title: Targeted workup after initial febrile urinary tract infection: using a novel machine learning model to identify children most likely to benefit from voiding cystourethrogram
contribution: An optimal classification tree trained on the RIVUR placebo arm and CUTIE (500 children) after optimal tree imputation predicts recurrent febrile UTI with reflux from pre-VCUG data (test AUC 0.761) and is proposed to target VCUG after a first UTI.
problem_entry: {ML AP} The AAP 2011 guideline defers VCUG until a second UTI unless ultrasound is abnormal, but ultrasound correlates poorly with reflux; the entry is to predict the joint outcome (recurrent febrile UTI and VUR) from data available before VCUG (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: OptImpute, then OptimalTrees with oversampling and weighting; train/validation/test with 5-fold cross-validation; interactions made a priori; invasive (serum) variables dropped; fewer than 8 variables per patient (pp. 2, 4-7).
assumptions: 500 children (305 RIVUR placebo, 195 CUTIE), 90% female, 53 positives (10.6%); ages 2 months to 6 years; congenital anomalies excluded (pp. 2, 4-5, 7).
proof_devices: n/a: no formulation of its own; OCT and OptImpute used by reference (p. 5)
experiments: Test AUC 0.761 (0.714-0.808) (pp. 2, 6); other learners only in an appendix not in the file (p. 6); no comparison with the AAP rule and no decision-level numbers; leaf probabilities of 76.4-100% (high-risk) and 0-23.3% (low-risk) against a 10.6% base rate and a 0.5 cutoff, with no statement on recalibration after oversampling (pp. 13, 17); Julia 0.6.0, Python 2.7.13, SAS 9.4 (p. 5).
positioning: Framed against the controversial all-or-none AAP 2011 guideline (pp. 2-3); claims to be the first ML model predicting clinical outcomes in children with UTI (p. 6).
writing: Clinical structure with group authorship (p. 2); worked patient examples to show interpretability (pp. 5-6); candid limits, calling the model imperfect (p. 7).
limits_future: Age range, female predominance and exclusions limit generalizability; a small cohort, so the model is imperfect (p. 7); further validation needed, especially for urine ACR (p. 8); a webpage and an app (p. 8).

method_links.note: Names the decision (VCUG now or defer) and the incumbent AAP 2011 rule, but scores predictions only (AUC); neither the guideline nor the model's VCUG decisions are scored.
The duel with logistic regression, random forests and boosted trees sits in an appendix not in the file; no solver, limit or certificate details.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: clinical pipeline: optimal imputation, OCT, public web tool
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: OptImpute, OptimalTrees and a free webpage with an app pending; S231 follows the same pipeline.

transferable: Define the outcome as the conjunction that makes the test worth doing (reflux together with recurrent febrile infection), not as the test's finding alone (p. 4).
Drop variable groups that need invasive tests when model performance barely changes, and cap the per-patient variable count (p. 6).
coauthors: Jack Dunn, Michael Li, Daisy Zhuo (MIT ORC Personalized Medicine Group); Carlos Estrada, Caleb Nelson, Hsin-Hsiao Scott Wang (Boston Children's Hospital)

quotes.text: Unlike many machine learning techniques with “black-box” reputation, OCT models enable physicians to look “under the hood” while maintaining high performance.
It is important to recognize that this prediction model is imperfect, primarily due to the inherent size limitation.

title: Clinical benefit, toxicity and cost of metastatic breast cancer therapies: systematic review and meta-analysis
contribution: A systematic review of 1,865 Phase II-III metastatic breast cancer drug trials (2,676 arms, 184,563 patients), synthesized by network meta-analysis, random-effects meta-analysis and lasso-standardized meta-analysis in 14 strata, published with drug costs as a public web tool (cancertrials.info) and checked prospectively on the next data pull.
problem_entry: {AP; no optimization} Clinicians, trialists and guideline designers need fast reviews; guidelines omit many trials and NMAs cover subsets and RCTs only; the entry is all Phase II-III trials, randomized or not, with costs, in a web tool (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: In each stratum: NMA of RCT hazard ratios and DLT risk differences, random-effects meta-analysis of all arms, and lasso standardization of arm outcomes to the stratum's average population (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Searches from Oct 2012 to Mar 2019, protocol not registered (p. 2); DLT from CTCAE grades; costs from Medicare ASP or GoodRx (p. 3); exponential survival for variances; mean imputation (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: n/a: no proofs; method-of-moments and DerSimonian-Laird random effects, I-squared, lasso with 10-fold cross-validation (pp. 3-4)
experiments: R 3.4.3 with caret, glmnet and netmeta (p. 4); 42 NMAs with average I-squared 22-29%, up to 76-79% for toxicity (p. 5); standardization lowers the OS I-squared by 4% (p = 0.002) (p. 6); on the March 2019 pull 13 of 15 survival arms (87%) and 13 of 16 DLT arms (81%) fall within the earlier CIs, with the misses explained (p. 6).
positioning: Contrasted with ASCO and NCCN guidelines and with NMAs restricted to subsets; includes non-randomized arms to capture doses and populations (pp. 1-2).
writing: Use-case vignettes for an oncologist and a trialist (p. 8); itemized limitations (pp. 8-9); conclusions phrased as what the tool would enable (p. 1).
limits_future: Publication, search, blinding (15%) and reporting biases; unobserved confounding; variance assumptions; 42% of arms without median OS; cost heterogeneity (pp. 5, 8-9); future: monthly updates and other diseases (p. 9).

method_links.note: A trial database kept up over 2012-2019 by former MIT graduate students and MIT and Wellesley undergraduates, with monthly updates planned; matches Heuristic 6, the tie to the earlier database being inferred.
Built for therapy choice by survival, toxicity and cost, with NCCN recommendation status displayed, but it prescribes nothing and scores no decision against the guidelines.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: prospective re-check of synthesized estimates on the next data pull
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Estimates frozen at the March 2018 pull; coverage of the new arms checked on the March 2019 pull; misses traced to population differences.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: public web tool as the deliverable of a clinical paper
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: cancertrials.info; S231 ships a web tool and S281 a webpage and app.

transferable: Freeze the synthesized estimates at one data pull, test the coverage of the next pull's new arms and explain each miss (pp. 4, 6).
Standardize arm-level outcomes to a stratum's typical population with lasso on confounders before pooling, and report what this does to heterogeneity (pp. 3-4, 6).
List the biases specific to the data asset one by one, with how much each could matter, such as the 42% of arms with no median OS (pp. 8-9).

quotes.text: In 13 of these arms (87%), the 95% confidence intervals for the standardized outcome from the new study arm overlapped the 95% confidence intervals from the meta-analyses for all survival outcomes in all relevant strata.
This unobserved confounding can bias the resulting estimates of median overall survival, median PFS/TTP, and DLT proportion for drug combinations.

title: Covariate-adaptive optimization in online clinical trials
contribution: CA-RO, an online robust MIO for assigning sequentially arriving trial subjects, treats future covariates as uncertain in an ellipsoid, solves each step exactly by closed-form worst cases and enumeration, keeps randomization's bias protections by drawing Gamma at random, and in nonlinear-response settings reaches 80% power with 25-50% fewer subjects than the best covariate-adaptive randomization.
problem_entry: {RO IO; AP} Randomization risks accidental covariate imbalance; the online state of the art is biased coins and matching; the offline OPT needs all covariates; the entry is to treat future arrivals as uncertain parameters (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: At each arrival, minimize the largest pairwise discrepancy in means and approximate variances with future covariates in an ellipsoid around the running mean and covariance (pp. 4-5); closed-form worst cases turn each step into an enumeration of complexity 2^(mr), independent of N (pp. 3, 5); aggregation CA-RO(r), with CA-RO(N) = OPT (pp. 5-6); Gamma drawn from [0.5, 4] at each step and set to 0 near the end (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: N and k known; exchangeable arrivals; normalized covariates (pp. 3-4); the Mayo PBC trial (312 patients, three of 20 covariates) (p. 7); synthetic NL, LIN and NR response models with two N(0,1) covariates and noise sd 0.75 (p. 9).
proof_devices: closed-form worst cases of linear and quadratic functions over an ellipsoid by KKT conditions and eigenvalue optimization (p. 5; details in the e-companion, not read)
randomization test under Fisher's sharp null for power and Type I error (p. 8)
Proposition 1: Lipschitz bounds on the imbalance in unseen factors through matching problems (pp. 11-12; proof not read)
Weierstrass extension to continuous functions on compact supports (p. 12)
experiments: Lowest first- and second-moment imbalance among the online methods (Table 1, p. 7); power at N = 40, 80, 120: no gain under NR, equal after adjustment under LIN, large gains under NL (p. 9); 80% power with 58 vs 122 subjects per group at delta0 = 0.75 and 22 vs 30 at 1.75 against Pocock-Simon (pp. 9-10); Type I error 6.5-7.1% at N = 40, below Pocock-Simon (pp. 10-11); under one second per assignment (p. 6); no assignment sequence above 6% likelihood (p. 10).
positioning: Extends the Bertsimas-Johnson-Kallus 2015 offline OPT to online arrivals; set against biased coin designs, Kapelner-Krieger matching and Bhat et al.'s DP; answers Efron's three advantages of randomization (pp. 2-3, 10-12).
writing: Four-item benefits list (p. 3); the abstract leads with the 25-50% sample-size reduction, presented as one setting (p. 2); a practical-considerations list with defaults (p. 6).
limits_future: Gains concentrate in nonlinear-response settings (p. 9); certifiability trades against selection bias (pp. 10-11); the allocation distribution is not uniform (p. 12); outlier exclusion left to future work (p. 6); no real trial run; Type I error above 5% at N = 40 not discussed (p. 11).

method_links.note: The decision metric is power and sample size against the randomization rules the field uses, turned into trial cost and duration; no field test.
Duels the incumbent randomization designs and prints where the method does not help (NR; LIN after adjustment); no warm start or certificate, since enumeration is exact.
The robust model leaves commercial solver classes; exactness is kept by closed-form worst cases and an enumeration independent of N.
Gamma is not priced but randomized to keep randomization's bias protection; a fixed Gamma trades that for certifiability.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: randomized robustness parameter as a randomization device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Gamma drawn uniformly from [0.5, 4] at each step yields many distinct allocations (none above 6% likelihood) while keeping balance; a fixed Gamma gives certifiability.
Minimum subjects per group for 80% power (58 vs 122 at delta0 = 0.75); also S224 (ambulances) and S231 (CT scans).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact special-purpose algorithm when the formulation leaves solver classes
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Closed-form worst cases plus an enumeration of at most m scenarios, complexity independent of N; also S184 (custom branch-and-bound).

transferable: Model future arrivals as uncertain parameters in an ellipsoid around the running sample mean and covariance; solve the worst cases in closed form and enumerate the current assignment (pp. 4-5).
Randomize the robustness parameter at each step to keep randomization's bias protection, and fix it when certifiability matters more (pp. 5, 10-11).
Report power under several hidden response models with both unadjusted and regression-adjusted estimators, so the regimes where the method does not help are visible (p. 9).
Evaluate against the rival school's own criteria (Efron's freedom from selection bias, freedom from accidental bias, reasoned basis for inference) (pp. 3, 10-12).

quotes.text: Formulation (2) takes the form of a mixed-binary quadratic robust optimization problem with conic uncertainty set, which cannot be solved using off-the-shelf commercial solvers.

However, post hoc regression adjustment using ordinary least squares, which exactly replicates the covariate-response model with additive treatment effect, reduces the need for the a priori covariate balance provided by CA-RO.
